title: The Mock Caliph

full_text:
One evening, the Caliph Harun al-Rashid, disguised as an ordinary merchant alongside his vizier Ja'afar and Masrur, sailed down the Tigris in a small rowing boat to inspect the peace of his capital. As their boat drifted beneath the grand arched bridge, they saw a magnificent royal barge approaching, illuminated with hundreds of lanterns and silk banners.

Upon the gilded deck sat a young man dressed in the exact robes, black turban, and mantle of the Caliph! Beside him stood a mock vizier, a mock executioner, and fifty armed attendants who treated him with imperial deference. The young mock-caliph listened to petitions, distributed sacks of gold to the poor boatmen, and held court with regal majesty.

Harun al-Rashid was astonished. 'Who is this bold youth who dares to play the Caliph upon my own river?' he whispered to Ja'afar.

The next morning, the Caliph sent guards to arrest the mock-caliph and bring him to the palace. The youth, whose name was Mohammed Ali, was brought in chains before the real throne. He turned pale with terror, fell prostrate to the marble floor, and pleaded for his life.

'Explain yourself!' commanded Harun al-Rashid. 'Why did you mimic my sacred office?'

Mohammed Ali wept and confessed: 'O Commander of the Faithful, I am the son of a wealthy jeweler who left me an enormous fortune. Having neither wife nor children, I dreamed of feeling the joy of a monarch who delivers justice and wipes away the tears of the poor. Every evening, I hired musicians and distributed my father’s gold to the destitute, pretending to be you, whom I revere above all men! I had no treason in my heart, only a foolish desire to play at benevolence.'

Harun al-Rashid smiled at the youth’s extraordinary confession. 'Your intention was generous,' said the Caliph, 'yet authority without responsibility causes confusion in the realm. From this day forward, you shall not play the Caliph upon a boat; I appoint you my royal almoner, and you shall distribute my own imperial treasury to the needy every Friday.' Thus the youth’s dream became reality through lawful duty.
moral: Generosity and theatrical playfulness must never overstep the boundaries of civic order and respect for law.

quiz.question: What is the central moral lesson taught in "The Mock Caliph"?
options: Presence of mind and quiet wisdom triumph over brute strength.
Acting in haste and anger without thinking
Believing rumors and flattery without proof
